lessons.title: vim: modes and the first keys
lessons.goal:
Learn what vim's modes are and the small set of keys that is enough to edit any file on any server.

Why it matters: on a minimal server, in rescue mode, or over a slow SSH link, `vi` or `vim` is often the only editor you have.

setup.note: Vim is interactive. For the outputs we drive it with scripts (`-Nes -u NONE -c ...`), which run exactly the keys you would type. Use a scratch directory.

steps.title: vi is almost always there
steps.text: `vi` is part of the POSIX tools, so even tiny systems have it. `vim` is the improved version, and often `vi` is a link to it.

run.output: VIM - Vi IMproved 8.2 (2019 Dec 12, compiled Jul 29 2026 00:00:00)

steps.title: Modes decide what a key does
steps.text:
Vim has **modes**. In **Normal** mode keys are commands (`dd` deletes a line). In **Insert** mode keys are text. Press `i` to enter Insert and `Esc` to return. `:` opens the command line (**Command-line** mode). `v` starts **Visual** mode to select text.

The start is Normal mode. When you are lost, press `Esc` twice.

run.reason: vim needs an interactive terminal; the next steps drive the same keys from a script

steps.title: Keys are commands: a scripted proof
steps.text: `-Nes -u NONE` starts vim silent, without compatibility mode and without any config, so the result is repeatable. `-c` runs a command. `normal KEYS` types the keys in Normal mode. Silent Ex mode starts on the **last** line, so we begin with `gg` (go to the first line). Then `j` moves down and `dd` deletes the line.

run.cmd: vim -Nes -u NONE -c 'normal ggjdd' -c 'wq' n.txt; cat n.txt

steps.under: `:wq` writes the buffer to the file and quits. Vim edits a **buffer** in memory. The file on disk changes only when you write.

steps.title: Copy, paste, undo, insert
steps.text: `yy` copies (yanks) a line, `p` pastes after, `P` before, `u` undoes, `x` deletes a character. `O` opens a new line above and enters Insert mode. In the script, the text after `O` is typed in Insert mode, and the end of the command acts like `Esc`.

run.cmd: vim -Nes -u NONE -c 'normal ggyyP' -c 'normal ggOnew first line' -c 'wq' n.txt; cat n.txt
run.output:
new first line
one
one
three
four

steps.title: Search and replace
steps.text: `:%s/old/new/g` replaces in the whole file (`%` = all lines, `g` = every match on the line). `:g/pattern/d` deletes every line that matches.

steps.title: Save and quit
steps.text: Type these in Normal mode, they start with `:`. `:w` write, `:q` quit, `:wq` or `:x` write and quit, `:q!` quit and **discard** changes, `u` undo, `Ctrl-r` redo, `/text` search, `n` next match.

run.reason: typed inside an interactive vim session

quiz.q: You opened a file in vim and typing letters does nothing useful. Which mode are you in?
quiz.explain: In Normal mode keys are commands. Press `i` to type text.

quiz.q: How do you leave vim and throw away your changes?
What does `dd` do in Normal mode?
quiz.explain: It deletes (and yanks) the current line.

quiz.q: Why did the scripted examples start with `normal gg`?
options: Silent Ex mode starts on the last line
quiz.explain: Otherwise `j` cannot move down from the last line.

check.scenario: You edited /etc/hosts as root in vim, made a mess and want to start over without saving. What do you press?
check.answer: `Esc` (to be sure you are in Normal mode), then `:q!` and Enter. Nothing is written. If you already saved, undo with `u` until the text is right and save again, or restore from a backup.

lessons.title: vim: operators, motions, macros, filters, and nano
lessons.goal:
Learn vim's grammar (operator + motion), repeating with `.`, recording macros, filtering through shell commands, and what to use when you only have nano.

Why it matters: with the grammar you combine a few commands instead of memorising hundreds, and macros turn a 100-line edit into one command.

setup.note: Vim is interactive. For the outputs we drive it with scripts (`-Nes -u NONE -c ...`), which run exactly the keys you would type. Use a scratch directory.

steps.title: Operator + motion
steps.text: A command is an **operator** (`d` delete, `c` change, `y` yank) plus a **motion** (`w` next word, `$` end of line, `}` next paragraph) or a **text object** (`iw` inner word, `i"` inside quotes). A count multiplies: `d2w` deletes two words.

run.cmd: printf 'one two three four\n' > w.txt; vim -Nes -u NONE -c 'normal ggwd2w' -c 'wq' w.txt; cat w.txt
printf 'say "old" now\n' > q.txt; vim -Nes -u NONE -c 'normal ggf"ci"new' -c 'wq' q.txt; cat q.txt

steps.title: The dot repeats the last change
steps.text: `.` repeats the last change in Normal mode. Make one change, move, press `.` again.

run.cmd:
printf 'a
b
c
' > d.txt; vim -Nes -u NONE -c 'normal ggx' -c 'normal j.' -c 'wq' d.txt; cat d.txt

steps.title: Macros
steps.text: A **macro** is a register that holds keys. In the editor, `qa` records into register `a`, `q` stops, `@a` replays it, `3@a` replays three times. Here we fill the register with a script and replay it: append `;` to a line and move down.

run.cmd:
printf 'a
b
c
' > k.txt; vim -Nes -u NONE -c 'let @a = "A;\<Esc>j"' -c 'normal gg3@a' -c 'wq' k.txt; cat k.txt

steps.title: Filter lines through any shell command
steps.text: `:%!cmd` sends the whole buffer to `cmd` and replaces it with the output. Anything in your shell toolbox becomes an editor command: `sort -u` here.

run.cmd:
printf 'c
a
b
a
' > s.txt; vim -Nes -u NONE -c '%!sort -u' -c 'wq' s.txt; cat s.txt

steps.title: Global commands
steps.text: `:g/pattern/cmd` runs `cmd` on every matching line. `:g/^$/d` removes empty lines, `:g/foo/s/a/b/` substitutes only on lines with foo, and `:v/foo/d` deletes lines that do **not** match.

run.cmd:
printf 'x

y


z
' > e.txt; vim -Nes -u NONE -c 'g/^$/d' -c 'wq' e.txt; cat e.txt

steps.title: nano as a fallback
steps.text: `nano` shows its commands at the bottom (`^` means Ctrl): `Ctrl-O` write out, `Ctrl-X` exit, `Ctrl-W` search. There are no modes. Programs such as `visudo` and `crontab -e` start the editor named in `$VISUAL` or `$EDITOR`, so you can choose.

run.reason: crontab -e opens an interactive editor on your own crontab

steps.under: `:%!cmd` works like a pipeline: vim writes the lines to the command's stdin and reads its stdout back. That is why every Unix filter works inside vim.

quiz.q: What does `ci"` do in Normal mode?
options: Changes the text inside the quotes
quiz.explain: `c` is the change operator and `i"` the text object inside quotes.

options: Sorts the buffer through the sort command
Deletes duplicates in the file name
quiz.explain: The whole buffer is replaced by the command's output.

quiz.q: How do you repeat the last change?
quiz.explain: The dot repeats the last change.

quiz.q: Which variable chooses the editor for `visudo` and `crontab -e`?
quiz.explain: The programs start the editor named there.

check.scenario: A config file has 300 lines `foo=1` and you must change each to `foo=2`, but only in the section after the line `[prod]`. Which vim approach is safest?
check.answer: Use a range: `:/\[prod\]/,$s/foo=1/foo=2/gc` (the `c` asks before each change). `/\[prod\]/,$` is the range from the next `[prod]` line to the end of the file. Review with `:w !diff % -` or keep a backup first.

interview.a: Normal (commands), Insert (typing text), Command-line (`:` commands), Visual (selection), plus Replace. See [the lesson](#/lesson/6/vim-first-keys).

interview.q: How do you quit vim without saving?

interview.a: Commands combine an operator (d, c, y) with a motion or text object (w, $, ip, i"). `d2w`, `ci"`, `y}` follow one grammar, so you learn parts, not hundreds of commands. See [the lesson](#/lesson/6/vim-operators-macros).

interview.q: How can you run a shell command on the whole buffer?
interview.a: `:%!command`, for example `:%!sort -u`. The buffer goes to the command's stdin and is replaced with its stdout.

interview.q: Why does a terminal editor still matter for admins?
interview.a: It is on every server and works over slow SSH and in recovery mode, where no GUI editor exists.

glossary.def: The in-memory text vim edits. The file changes only when written.
Vim's default mode, where keys are commands.
A vim command that acts on a motion: d (delete), c (change), y (yank).
A named storage slot for text or macro keys (a to z, and special ones).
A recorded sequence of keys stored in a register and replayed with @.
Environment variable naming the editor that programs such as visudo start.
